# A. Bottleneck Assignment

## How to find it

Binary-search the threshold at which a perfect bipartite matching first exists.

## Correctness

Feasibility is monotone and equivalent to an assignment with maximum cost at most the threshold.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

There are logarithmically many threshold decisions, each one bipartite
matching. Feasibility is monotone because raising the threshold only adds
edges; without that sentence, binary search has not been justified.

# B. Roommate Rescue

## How to find it

Use a maximum matching in the compatibility graph.

## Correctness

Each matched edge covers exactly two participants, so maximum edge count minimizes the unmatched remainder.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

General matching takes `O(n cubed)` in the reference. The final number is
`n-2*matching_size`; maximizing the number of edges and maximizing covered
vertices are equivalent because matching edges are disjoint.

# C. Cut Threshold Pairs

## How to find it

Enumerate and sort all Gomory--Hu path minima.

## Correctness

Each stored value is exactly one unordered pair cut, so upper bound answers every threshold count.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

After the `n-1` flows used to build the cut tree, the reference extracts all
pair path minima in `O(n cubed)` and answers each threshold by binary search.
This is appropriate for the stated size; larger limits would call for
offline tree-edge aggregation rather than changing the cut-tree theorem.

# D. Rainbow Spanning Tree

## How to find it

Seek common independent size `n-1` in graphic and color matroids.

## Correctness

A forest of `n-1` edges is spanning, making the size test necessary and sufficient.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

The target size matters: graphic independence only promises a forest, and
partition independence only promises distinct colors. Reaching exactly
`n-1` turns the forest into a spanning tree and completes the equivalence.

# E. Broadcast Backbone

## How to find it

Apply directed minimum-arborescence contraction with signed reduced costs.

## Correctness

Loops and parallel or negative edges do not alter the minimum-incoming/cycle replacement proof.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

The implementation is `O(VE)`. Negative weights are harmless because each
contraction charges mandatory incoming minima and carries only replacement
costs onward; reachability from the root remains a separate feasibility issue.

# F. Two-Map Forest

## How to find it

Seek size `n-1` in two graphic matroids.

## Correctness

That size is a spanning tree on both n-vertex maps, and every common spanning tree is such a common independent set.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

Both endpoint maps must have the same vertex count stated by the problem, but
their connectivity evolves independently. A common independent set of size
below `n-1` is not a partial answer: it certifies that no common spanning tree
exists only after matroid intersection has reached maximum cardinality.

# Mixed-contest stress plan

Use permutation enumeration for A, recursive matching enumeration for B,
pairwise max flow for C, subset enumeration for D and F, and incoming-edge
enumeration for E. Generate both feasible and impossible targets. This set is
particularly sensitive to reductions that are almost right, so compare the
reported optimum as well as the validity of any reconstructed object.
